facts.text: The human-machine interface (HMI) comprises everything through which the system and operator communicate, including screens, lights, sounds, vibrations and buttons in the cab.
facts.quote: The human-machine interface (HMI) is everything through which the system and the operator communicate: the screens, lights, sounds, vibrations and buttons in the cab.

facts.text: A good human-machine interface makes urgent warnings unmistakable, shows the object's location, and lets the operator acknowledge or override without fumbling.
facts.quote: A good HMI makes the urgent warning unmistakable, shows where the object is, and lets the operator acknowledge or override without fumbling.

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 requires warning levels that can be distinguished from one another.
facts.quote: ISO 21815-3 requires warning levels that can be told apart [Chapter 8].

facts.text: The Australian ACARP project tested visual and auditory proximity interfaces in a haul-truck simulator and found that a schematic display helped drivers reduce collision risk.
facts.quote: The Australian ACARP project tested visual and auditory proximity interfaces in a haul-truck simulator and found that a schematic display helped drivers reduce collision risk [Chapters 1, 4].

facts.text: People on foot responded fastest to vibration signals, followed by visual signals and then sound.
facts.quote: People on foot responded fastest to vibration, then visual signals, then sound [Chapter 4].

facts.text: Workers rated underground proximity systems positively for training, ease of use and feedback, but negatively for reliability and fit with the task.
facts.quote: Workers rated underground proximity systems well on training, ease of use and feedback, and poorly on reliability and fit with the task [Chapter 4].

facts.text: The continuous audible warning in the haul-truck radar study was sufficiently annoying to be switched off.
facts.quote: The continuous audible warning in the haul-truck radar study was annoying enough to be switched off [Chapter 4].

facts.text: During testing, every warning should be logged with its level, time stamp, audio, visual or haptic state, and acknowledgement.
facts.quote: For testing, every warning should be logged with its level, time stamp, audio, visual or haptic state and acknowledgement

facts.text: Without logging warning level, time stamp, audio, visual or haptic state and acknowledgement, testers cannot determine afterward whether a warning was given, seen and ignored.
facts.quote: otherwise it is impossible to tell afterward whether a warning was given, seen and ignored [Chapter 7].

facts.text: The human-machine interface determines whether the warning stage of a staged intervention gives the operator real time to respond.
facts.quote: The HMI decides whether the warning stage of a staged intervention buys the operator real time

facts.text: The human-machine interface determines whether an automatic stop surprises the operator.
facts.quote: The HMI decides whether the warning stage of a staged intervention buys the operator real time, and whether an automatic stop surprises the operator.

facts.text: The booklet recommends resolving basic human-machine interface problems in a simulator before expensive prototype tests.
facts.quote: The booklet recommends sorting out basic HMI problems in a simulator before expensive prototype tests [Chapter 1].
